articles.title: The Doomsday Team Recalled Patrick Stewart’s Last Day On Set, And I’m Going To Need A Tissue
articles.summary: I don't think I'm ready for this emotional goodbye.
articles.content:
I've been looking forward to seeing Sir Patrick Stewart return as Professor Charles Xavier in Avengers: Doomsday , especially knowing he'll be sharing the screen with Sir Ian McKellen again. The two actors have been part of the X-Men franchise for more than 25 years, and I can't imagine the flick without them. Although after Stewart's death in October , his final appearance will carry considerably more emotional weight than anyone originally anticipated. Now Marvel Studios president Kevin Feige and directors Joe and Anthony Russo are opening up about Stewart's last day on set for the upcoming Marvel movie , and I'm already getting emotional.

Well, that got me. Stewart died at 86 on Oct. 29, making Doomsday his final on-screen performance . Knowing he apparently recognized the significance of that moment makes the story particularly heartbreaking.

The director also revealed that Stewart was dealing with significant health challenges while filming. According to Russo, the actor's determination to deliver the performance was evident to everyone around him. And it wasn't easy watching someone they admired push himself so hard. He continued:

I have a feeling that sentiment will carry over to audiences when the film finally arrives. Stewart first portrayed Xavier in the 2000s X-Men , eventually becoming one of the franchise's most recognizable faces. He returned for several sequels, delivered a particularly devastating performance in 2017's Logan, and later surprised MCU fans with an appearance in Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness .

Now, more than a quarter-century after his first appearance, he'll be returning alongside McKellen's Magneto. Joe Russo revealed that the longtime friends share an emotional scene about forgiveness, which could be especially difficult to watch under the circumstances.

articles.title: Spider-Man/Hulk: Fire and Brimstone #4 Is Everything You Could Want From a Penultimate Story (Review)
articles.summary: Marvel has been all about putting Spider-Man and the Hulk together this summer, for obvious reasons. Spider-Man: Brand New Day was a smash hit, owning the summer box office, so Marvel Studios made Marvel Comics (yes, yes, Feige would never mandate MCU synergy, which has been getting more prevalent since he took over Marvel overall; […]
articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google Marvel has been all about putting Spider-Man and the Hulk together this summer, for obvious reasons. Spider-Man: Brand New Day was a smash hit, owning the summer box office, so Marvel Studios made Marvel Comics (yes, yes, Feige would never mandate MCU synergy, which has been getting more prevalent since he took over Marvel overall; I'm sure that's a coincidence) put out a whole lot Spider-Man/Hulk comics, putting some of their best talent out there. If you've read one story starring ol'Jade Jaws and Spidey, you've basically read them all. Well, until Spider-Man/Hulk: Fire and Brimstone, from writers Kevin Smith and Andy McElfresh and artist R.B. Silva, that is.

Spider-Man/Hulk: Fire and Brimstone #1 kicked off a unique take on the two heroes' relationship. This time, Hulk was in town to get his demons exorcised… literally. Cardinal Thornhill had been performing miracles and Bruce Banner actually believed the Hulk could exorcised from him, with Spider-Man getting involved to make sure it was on the up and up. It was awesome, exactly the kind of thing that Catholic writer Kevin Smith does so well, with issues two and three building up to the exorcism. Issue #4 takes place after that moment and it's basically an example of how to do an penultimate chapter in the Kevin Smith way.

Spider-Man is Marvel's most relatable hero and Kevin Smith is comics' most relatable nerd. Smith was able to show that cool people also liked superheroes when they were adults and he showed an entire generation of comic fans how to act in public (Brody from Mallrats was somewhat toxic, but he had the capacity for change and was able to get girlfriends, which was a legit worry of being a teen male comic nerd in the '90s). Smith's comic wors is much like his movies – punchy quips, sarcasm, and well drawn-out characters, and Fire and Brimstone had those in spades. The fourth issue is a perfect example of Smith's work and why it's so enjoyable for a certain generation of readers.

Smith came up reading the Bronze Age comics of the '70s and '80s. Those books were wordy, but they were wordy in a different way. Stan Lee narrated panels, but writers in the Bronze Age allowed the artists to draw and dealt with the feelings and the drama. Smith writes in that style, and this issue is a perfect example of how he makes that work. I try not to spoil stories too much, but this issue is all about Spidey showing off why he's more than just a guy who follows his spider-sense and punches people. He breaks down how he knew the exorcism was fake and then takes apart the villains in a fight in that way that only he can. Smith and McElfresh are able to pace this story out perfectly; this is a story with a lot of exposition, but the writers keep it all buoyant, funny, and exciting.

Penultimate stories are all about showing the readers the mechanisms of the plan and the hero finally putting the pieces together, revealing the villain's final plan. An argument can be made that the mastermind behind this scheme was pretty easy to figure out, but Smith and McElfresh have packed this issue with other surprises. The scheme honestly ends up being a rather tried and true one that villain use against the Hulk, but the way Smith and McElfresh were able to obscure that throughout the run of the book makes it all worth it. I complain a lot about creators doing the same old stories, but it's impossible in comics not to always do the same old stories.

The best creators are able to take these cliche stories and package them in such a way where at first, you don't realize where things are going, and by the time you do, it's a welcome twist. Smith and McElfresh pull that off with this issue and I love it. Sure, the cliche is still there, but I didn't read four issues of cliches. I read almost four issues of a story that I hadn't gotten before before it turned into something familiar.

R.B. Silva has definitely reached a new level of stardom in the 2020s. Silva has been soldiering along in the industry building his style and Powers of X put him in the biggest X-book of the last seven years. Fans loved his work in that comic, ensuring his bright future Since that book, he's been getting the big books and showing why he should be trusted with them. His style has a cartoonish quality to it that I love – especially when he's colored by color artists like Powers of X 's Marte Gracia or Federico Blee. Blee is another artist who has been doing some of the best work of career this decade, working with some of the most in-demand artists around and making them look like a million bucks.

This is an issue that combines exposition with action, and Silva and Blee are able to make it work. My only problem with the issue's art is that Silva packs every panel and sometimes, it's just too much. However, it's a minor complaint. His character acting gets the point across – he's even able to get across how Spider-Man feels without showing his face – his figure work is gorgeous, and his action is hard-hitting and fluid. Silva draws an awesome Hulk, a mountain of green muscle, with that classic monster face and bowl cut. We get some cool transformation sequences, some fights that prove that the Hulk is the strongest one there is , and an awesome last page that will hype you up for the next issue.

Spider-Man/Hulk: Fire and Brimstone has been an interesting ride. Smith and McElfresh crafted a fun Spider-Man/Hulk story that took us in some fun theological directions before it came around to a more standard Hulk plot to close out the tale. This issue is a well-paced, entertaining little yarn, with great humor and cool little twists hitting readers constantly. The art is fantastic, but not flawless, bringing the script to life adroitly. I feel like this book is going to be one that will have a long second life; it's great month to month, but I can't wait to read it in one go. This issue does a fantastic job of preparing readers for a furious finale in the mighty Marvel manner, even if it's not completely flawless.

Spider-Man/Hulk: Fire and Brimstone #4 is on sale now.

Do you like the way Smith and McElfresh set up this story or would you have preferred they did it in another way? Sound off in the comment section below.

Studio Ufotable has been busy the last few years with all sorts of new projects now in various stages of development. But while fans are waiting on the next step in the Infinity Castle trilogy, the studio just hit theaters in Japan with their newest work adapting a major classic from TYPE-MOON's library .

Studio Ufotable has had plenty of experience adapting TYPE-MOON's various visual novel releases like the extended Fate/stay night franchise, and are currently making their way through theaters across Japan with a new feature film adaptation of Witch on the Holy Night. And to celebrate its current success in theaters in the region over its opening, it's now been announced that Witch on the Holy Night has a new sequel film in the works too.

───────────── 劇場アニメーション #魔法使いの夜 続編制作発表 ───────────── 現在公開中の『魔法使いの夜』を ぜひ劇場のスクリーンでお楽しみください！ そして、続編へと続く今後の展開にも ぜひご期待ください！ #TYPEMOON … pic.twitter.com/BqdFDWW4s5

Witch on the Holy Night is currently working its way through theaters in Japan, and it's doing quite well at the box office there so far. It's earned a little over three million USD in its first weekend alone, and it's been deemed a success by the studio as a result . Which also means they can now move forward on its sequel, but no release window or date has been announced for it at this time. That's likely also further complicated with Ufotable's ongoing work on the Demon Slayer: Kimetsu no Yaiba Infinity Castle trilogy, which has yet to confirm a release either.

It won't be too much longer before fans outside of Japan will be able to check it out for themselves as Crunchyroll and Sony Pictures Entertainment will be releasing the new film in the United States, Canada and more international territories on January 29th next yea r with both Japanese and English dubbed audio releases planned for the screenings. The English dub cast of the film has yet to be announced, but the Japanese voice cast from the original light novel are reprising their roles with Haruka Tomatsu as Aoko Aozaki, Kana Hanazawa as Alice Kuonji, and Yusuke Kobayashi as Soujyuro Shizuki confirmed.

Directed by Masashi Takeuchi for Ufotable, Witch on the Holy Night is based off of the TYPE-MOON visual novel originally written by Kinoko Nasu . This is the same creator behind the Fate/stay night franchise , and this story takes place before much of the extended universe of Nasu's other works so you won't need to do too much homework before jumping into the new movie. It's also going to feature the theme song titled "Yoru to Ao," as performed by supercell with Moe Tsuzuki providing the character designs, Manabu Kamino handling the editing, and Hideyuki Fukasawa composing the music.

Studio Ufotable has had a ton of experience bringing TYPE-MOON's various projects to life long before it even started the Demon Slayer: Kimetsu no Yaiba anime adaptation, and fans are now getting to see even more of their takes on it even with the success of its more blockbuster sibling. You might want to check this one out when it hits, but how do you feel about Witch on the Holy Night getting a sequel? Let us know your thoughts in the comments.
